lesson.title: Threat modeling trust boundaries and attack surfaces
lesson.why: Security controls work best when tied to a concrete asset and failure scenario. A list of tools does not explain who can submit untrusted input, where authority changes or how an attacker could turn a legitimate feature into unauthorized access.
lesson.what: Threat modeling describes a system, identifies what needs protection and examines how assumptions can fail. It produces prioritized mitigations and verification plans, not proof that every possible attack has been discovered.

concepts.name: Assets and flows
concepts.body: Start with valuable data, privileged operations and availability requirements. Draw processes, stores, external actors and data flows. A diagram should show where sensitive information travels and who can influence it, not merely the names of deployed products.

concepts.name: Trust boundaries
concepts.body: A boundary separates different authority or trust levels, such as an anonymous client and an authenticated API. Validate identity and input when crossing it. Internal network location alone does not guarantee that a caller or supplied object identifier is authorized.

concepts.name: Abuse cases
concepts.body: Ask how a feature could be misused: changing an object identifier, replaying a request or exhausting a queue. Distinguish the attacker's capability from the claimed outcome. Concrete preconditions make a threat actionable without requiring live exploitation.

concepts.name: Prioritization and evidence
concepts.body: Consider impact, plausible exposure and existing controls, documenting uncertainty rather than presenting arbitrary scores as measured risk. Each mitigation needs an owner and a testable acceptance condition. Revisit the model when interfaces, data sensitivity or deployment boundaries change.

e2e: Identify assets, legitimate workflows and actors with different authority.
Trace data and control flows across explicit trust boundaries.
Describe plausible abuse cases and rank them using documented assumptions.
Assign mitigations and verify that the intended unauthorized behavior is rejected safely.

tasks.name: Draw an order lookup
steps: Sketch a fictional browser, order API and order database. Mark the browser as untrusted and order records as sensitive. Identify the API-to-database lookup as the place where user identity must constrain which requested order can be returned.

tasks.name: Work an access decision
tasks.goal: Turn an abuse case into an expected result.
steps: Offline, user A owns order 101 and user B owns order 202. A asks for 202. Expected outcome is denial or a nonrevealing not-found response under the chosen contract, not a successful lookup merely because 202 exists.

tasks.name: Prioritize two threats
tasks.goal: Explain rather than invent a risk score.
steps: Compare cross-user order disclosure with a cosmetic page-layout bug. Prioritize disclosure because confidentiality and authorization fail. Record assumptions about reachable users and data sensitivity; do not claim a numerical likelihood without evidence or label every issue equally critical.

tasks.name: Specify mitigation evidence
steps: Write a test plan with permitted own-order access and denied other-order access using synthetic fixtures. Assign an owner and review trigger for adding administrator search. Explain why a network firewall alone cannot enforce object ownership inside an otherwise allowed API request.

key_terms: Asset: information or capability needing protection.
Trust boundary: transition between authority assumptions.
Attack surface: reachable inputs and interfaces.
Abuse case: plausible misuse of intended functionality.
lesson.safety: Use fictional assets and offline authorization tables. Do not probe live endpoints or attempt to access another person's records.
cleanup: Retain the sanitized model and acceptance criteria; no live system or personal data was used.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical order API is behind a firewall but returns any existing order ID to authenticated users. What threat remains?
interview_points: Authentication is not object-level authorization.
Model user-controlled identifiers crossing the API boundary.
Constrain queries by authorized ownership or role.
Test own-object success and cross-object denial with synthetic fixtures.

security/threat-modeling-trust-boundarie.core: Model assets, actors, flows and authority boundaries before selecting controls. Describe concrete abuse cases, rank them with explicit assumptions and pair each mitigation with an owner and safe acceptance tests.
objectives: Identify a trust boundary in an API flow.
Turn an abuse case into a verifiable authorization requirement.
prerequisites: Understand requests, identities and stored records.

storyboard.title: An allowed request can still target another user's order
storyboard.objective: Locate object authorization inside an authenticated flow.

scenes.title: Legitimate lookup
scenes.caption: The API must relate identity to the requested object.
scenes.narration: The user submits an order identifier. Authentication identifies the caller, but the API must still check ownership of that specific order.

scenes.title: Boundary assumption fails
scenes.caption: Existence alone is not permission.
scenes.narration: Order two hundred two exists but belongs to another user. Returning it based only on existence would cross the confidentiality boundary.

scenes.title: Enforce and test ownership
scenes.caption: Constrain the lookup and reject unauthorized access.
scenes.narration: The API applies ownership authorization and safely denies the request, while tests separately verify that the user's own order remains accessible.

lesson.title: Least privilege identity federation and access reviews
lesson.why: Long-lived broad credentials turn a small compromise into a larger incident. Federation can reduce stored secrets, but poorly constrained trust lets unintended callers obtain the same powerful role without ever knowing a password.
lesson.what: Least privilege grants only the actions, resources and conditions required for a task. Federation exchanges a trusted identity assertion for scoped access. Regular reviews reconcile granted privileges with current ownership, purpose and observed need.

concepts.name: Trust versus permission
concepts.body: A role's trust policy decides who may obtain it; its permissions decide what that session can do. Both boundaries need review. A narrow resource permission does not repair an overly broad trust relationship, and trusted identity does not imply unrestricted authority.

concepts.name: Federated claims
concepts.body: Validate issuer, audience and subject against expected values. Workload subjects can distinguish repository, branch or environment contexts. Accepting any subject from a large trusted issuer expands access beyond the intended workload even though the token signature is valid.

concepts.name: Session scope
concepts.body: Short-lived sessions reduce the window of credential reuse but remain powerful while valid. Scope actions and resources and apply appropriate conditions. Revocation behavior varies by system; do not assume changing a role immediately invalidates every already issued session.

concepts.name: Review and exception lifecycle
concepts.body: Review direct grants, group membership, federated trust and emergency access together. An unused permission is a candidate for removal, not automatic proof it is unnecessary during recovery. Document exceptions with owners, justification, expiry and evidence of periodic reassessment.

e2e: A workload authenticates to its expected identity issuer without storing a permanent access key.
The relying service validates token signature and required issuer, audience and subject claims.
A short-lived session receives only the allowed actions and resources.
Access evidence feeds periodic review, and stale grants or exceptions are removed through control procedures.

tasks.name: Evaluate claims offline
tasks.goal: Separate valid signature from permitted subject.
steps: A fictional trust accepts issuer I, audience deploy and subject project-A/release. A correctly signed token from I with subject project-B/test must be denied. Expected decision follows all required claims, not issuer signature alone.

tasks.name: Calculate effective permission scope
steps: A role allows read and write, but a session restriction permits only read. Assuming no other grants or denials, effective allowed action is read. Explain why adding a broad session token cannot legitimately bypass an explicit restriction at another required boundary.

tasks.name: Design a deployment role
steps: For a fictional artifact deployer, allow reading its approved artifact and updating only its own application environment. Exclude user administration and unrelated data stores. Name the actual service actions in a real implementation rather than inventing permissions for the deployment tool itself.

tasks.name: Review a stale exception
steps: A former contractor still belongs to an emergency administrator group. Flag ownership and current need, remove access through the approved process and inspect relevant use. Preserve a separate tested recovery path instead of leaving stale access solely because emergencies are possible.

key_terms: Federation: trust in an external identity assertion.
Audience: intended token recipient.
Subject: identity represented by a token.
Least privilege: minimum justified authority for a task.
lesson.safety: Use symbolic claims and action sets only. Do not inspect tokens, assume roles or modify real identity policies.
cleanup: Discard fictional sessions and retain the access-review checklist; no credentials were issued.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical workload uses OIDC instead of stored keys but trusts every repository from its issuer. Is its access adequately scoped?
interview_points: Verify audience and subject constraints as well as issuer.
Separate role trust from role action/resource permissions.
Use short sessions without assuming immediate universal revocation.
Review exceptions and stale memberships periodically.

security/least-privilege-identity-federa.core: Constrain both who can obtain a role and what it can do. Validate issuer, audience and subject. Short sessions reduce exposure but do not replace least privilege, access reviews and controlled emergency exceptions.
objectives: Evaluate federated trust claims.
Design meaningful least-privilege and review boundaries.
prerequisites: Understand authentication, authorization and role sessions.

storyboard.title: A valid token can have an unauthorized subject
storyboard.objective: Explain federation claim validation before role issuance.

scenes.title: Expected workload requests access
scenes.caption: Trust requires all intended claim constraints.
scenes.narration: The evaluator checks the token signature and required issuer, audience and workload subject before considering a role session.

scenes.title: Different subject arrives
scenes.caption: Issuer validity alone is insufficient.
scenes.narration: A token from the same issuer represents another project. Accepting it would expand access beyond the intended deployment identity.

scenes.title: Deny mismatched claims
scenes.caption: Only the expected identity receives scoped permissions.
scenes.narration: The trust rule rejects the mismatched subject and issues limited sessions only for approved claims, with permissions reviewed separately.

lesson.title: Secret management rotation and incident response
lesson.why: Replacing a secret in one configuration file does not ensure every consumer uses the new value or that the old value stopped working. Safe rotation coordinates issuer state, distribution, application reload and verification without exposing the secret itself.
lesson.what: Secret management protects issuance, storage, access and retirement of sensitive credentials. Rotation replaces active authority; incident response additionally assesses misuse, contains exposure and preserves evidence. A secret store is helpful but cannot correct excessive access by itself.

concepts.name: References and delivery
concepts.body: Applications should retrieve approved secret references through narrowly scoped identities rather than embedding values in source or images. Delivery can occur at startup or during operation. Each choice affects caching, reload behavior and the time required to adopt a replacement.

concepts.name: Planned overlap
concepts.body: Where the issuer supports two valid versions, introduce a replacement, move consumers, verify use and then revoke the old credential. Overlap avoids outages but temporarily leaves both valid. Some systems lack overlap support and require a different coordinated cutover.

concepts.name: Exposure containment
concepts.body: For a leaked credential, invalidate the exposed authority promptly according to incident severity rather than prioritizing a perfectly smooth rotation. Determine accessible resources and review use. Removing the visible copy does not erase logs, clones or copies already obtained.

concepts.name: Evidence and failure modes
concepts.body: Track secret version identifiers and consumer adoption without logging values. Failed reloads, stale connection pools and cached credentials can keep old authority in use. Verification should test authorized service behavior and rejection of the retired credential through approved safe procedures.

e2e: Identify the credential issuer, consumers, permissions and supported rotation mechanism.
Create or approve the replacement and distribute it through the secret-management path.
Verify consumer adoption and application health, then retire old authority according to the situation.
Review access evidence and remove leaked representations while documenting unresolved exposure.

tasks.name: Map consumers
steps: Draw a fictional API, background worker and scheduled report all using one database credential reference. Record whether each loads at startup or refreshes. Explain why updating only the API would leave the worker and report dependent on the old version.

tasks.name: Calculate overlap timing
steps: Assume all consumers refresh within 15 minutes and verification takes five more. A planned overlap must accommodate at least 20 minutes under those assumptions, plus chosen margin. This is a fictional scheduling bound, not a recommendation to delay revoking an actively abused credential.

tasks.name: Order leak response
steps: A fictional credential appears in a public log. Prioritize issuer-side containment, scope and access review, replacement distribution and cleanup of exposed representations. Do not paste the credential into a ticket or claim deleting the log invalidates copied values.

tasks.name: Design adoption evidence
steps: Create a table of consumer name, expected version label and last successful reload status. Use labels old and new, not credential strings. Flag an unrefreshed scheduled job as unresolved and require an approved check before declaring planned rotation complete.

key_terms: Secret reference: identifier used to retrieve protected material.
Rotation: replacing active credential authority.
Revocation: invalidating a credential.
Consumer: workload using a secret or credential.
lesson.safety: Use version labels only, never real secrets. Do not access secret stores, create credentials or test leaked tokens.
cleanup: Retain the fictional consumer checklist and discard mock incident details; no real secret lifecycle was changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical database secret was rotated successfully, but a scheduled job fails hours later. What likely dependency was missed?
interview_points: Identify every consumer and its refresh mechanism.
Check stale caches or startup-only loading.
Track version adoption without exposing values.
Separate planned overlap from urgent leak containment.

security/secret-management-rotation-and-.core: Rotate authority, not just stored text. Inventory consumers and refresh behavior, verify replacement adoption and retire old credentials. Leaks require prompt containment and use review; logs should contain version identifiers, never secret values.
objectives: Design a consumer-aware rotation sequence.
Distinguish planned rotation from exposure response.
prerequisites: Understand credential issuers, application configuration and caches.

storyboard.title: One forgotten consumer still uses the old secret
storyboard.objective: Trace rotation through issuer and application adoption.

scenes.title: Replacement available
scenes.caption: Publishing a new version does not update every process.
scenes.narration: The secret-management path makes a replacement available. Consumers adopt it according to their own refresh or startup behavior.

scenes.title: Scheduled job remains stale
scenes.caption: Retiring the old version can expose a missed dependency.
scenes.narration: The API has refreshed but the scheduled job retains its startup-loaded value. Its next execution fails when old authority is retired.

scenes.title: Verify the consumer inventory
scenes.caption: Track adoption with version labels and application checks.
scenes.narration: The operator reloads the intended consumer through the approved process and verifies adoption without logging secret values, completing the inventory check.

lesson.title: SAST DAST SCA and container vulnerability scanning
lesson.why: No scanner sees every class of weakness. Combining analysis techniques is useful only when teams understand what each result means, validate important findings and connect remediation evidence to the exact code or artifact that will run.
lesson.what: SAST analyzes source or compiled representations, DAST exercises a running application, SCA identifies dependency risk and image scanning examines container components. They overlap but expose different evidence, assumptions and operational hazards.

concepts.name: Static analysis
concepts.body: SAST can trace risky data flows or patterns without running a deployed service. It may lack configuration or runtime context and report false positives or miss dynamic behavior. Findings should identify the relevant path and a testable remediation rather than only a severity label.

concepts.name: Dynamic analysis
concepts.body: DAST observes responses from an executing target and can reveal deployed configuration problems. Its visibility depends on authentication, reachable routes and test coverage. Active scanning can modify data or stress services, so use explicitly authorized isolated targets and synthetic accounts.

concepts.name: Dependency analysis
concepts.body: SCA maps direct and transitive dependencies to advisories and sometimes license requirements. Accurate versions, lockfiles and vendor backports matter. A dependency inventory does not establish whether affected code is reachable, but absence of obvious reachability is not automatic dismissal.

concepts.name: Artifact triage
concepts.body: Container scanning inspects OS and application components within an image. Tie results to a digest and advisory snapshot. Prioritize exploitability, exposure, impact and available fixes, documenting accepted risk with owners and expiry instead of permanently suppressing inconvenient findings.

e2e: Choose analysis methods that match source, dependency, runtime and image risks.
Run them only within approved scope and record the analyzed revision or digest.
Validate significant findings using advisory and application context without unsafe exploitation.
Apply a fix, rerun relevant checks and track unresolved or accepted risk explicitly.

tasks.name: Match methods to risks
steps: Offline, map unsafe source data flow to SAST, missing deployed security headers to DAST, vulnerable transitive library to SCA and an outdated image package to container scanning. Explain one limitation for each rather than treating the categories as interchangeable products.

tasks.name: Calculate finding disposition
steps: A fictional batch has 20 findings: 12 confirmed fixed, three evidence-backed false positives and five open. Report 15 dispositions and five unresolved findings. Do not turn the count into a claim of 75 percent secure or assume undiscovered weaknesses do not exist.

tasks.name: Triage a version alert
steps: A scanner flags an older upstream version packaged with a distribution backport. Compare the full package release with the vendor advisory. Record evidence and scanner limitations; do not dismiss the finding solely because someone believes managed infrastructure handles all patching.

tasks.name: Design a safe DAST scope
steps: Specify an isolated disposable application, synthetic records, permitted routes, request limits and cleanup ownership. Exclude purchase, email and destructive administrative endpoints unless intentionally mocked. This exercise designs authorization and safety boundaries; it does not launch a scanner.

key_terms: SAST: static application security testing.
DAST: dynamic application security testing.
SCA: software composition analysis.
False positive: reported issue not applicable under verified conditions.
lesson.safety: Do not scan production, unknown hosts or real user data. No exploitation or active scanner execution is required.
cleanup: Retain synthetic triage decisions and scope; no scan jobs, accounts or target records were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical pipeline has a clean SAST result but deploys a vulnerable operating-system package. Why was this possible?
interview_points: SAST does not cover every packaged dependency or runtime component.
Add appropriate composition and image analysis.
Tie findings to actual artifact identity.
Treat clean results as scoped evidence, not proof of complete security.

security/sast-dast-sca-and-container-vul.core: SAST, DAST, SCA and image scanning observe different boundaries. Scope active tests safely, identify exact revisions and digests, validate advisories and triage with evidence. A clean scan or closed finding count is not a security guarantee.
objectives: Select analysis techniques by risk boundary.
Report evidence-based vulnerability dispositions honestly.
prerequisites: Understand source code, dependencies and deployed artifacts.

storyboard.title: A source scan does not inspect every image package

scenes.title: Source checks pass
scenes.caption: Evidence applies to the analyzed source paths.
scenes.narration: Static analysis reports no selected source issues. This is useful evidence but does not inspect every operating-system package shipped in the image.

scenes.title: Image advisory applies
scenes.caption: Another analysis boundary finds an affected component.
scenes.narration: Image analysis identifies a packaged library with an applicable advisory, so the release still has an unresolved risk despite its source result.

scenes.title: Triage the exact artifact
scenes.caption: Combine scoped results and verify the correction.
scenes.narration: The team confirms applicability, rebuilds the affected artifact and reruns relevant checks, retaining explicit unresolved findings instead of a blanket safe label.

lesson.title: SBOM signed artifacts provenance and supply-chain controls
lesson.why: Knowing an artifact's name is not enough to trust its origin or understand its contents. Supply-chain controls answer separate questions about component inventory, content identity, build history and the identities authorized to publish or deploy.
lesson.what: An SBOM inventories software components and relationships. Signatures bind identities to artifact statements, while provenance describes how an artifact was produced. Verification policies combine these records with immutable digests and protected build infrastructure.

concepts.name: Inventory scope
concepts.body: An SBOM can list direct and transitive components, versions and relationships. Its usefulness depends on completeness and connection to the actual artifact. Source-only inventory can miss runtime packages, and an inventory alone neither discovers every vulnerability nor proves exploitability.

concepts.name: Signature meaning
concepts.body: A signature provides cryptographic evidence under a trusted key or identity policy. Verify the artifact digest and expected signer, not just that some signature exists. A malicious artifact can be correctly signed by an unauthorized or compromised identity.

concepts.name: Build provenance
concepts.body: Provenance records selected inputs, builder identity and process details in a verifiable statement. Check that the expected repository and workflow produced the artifact. Self-asserted metadata from an untrusted build cannot independently establish that its claimed origin is true.

concepts.name: Enforcement and retention
concepts.body: A release gate can require approved provenance and signatures before promotion, with a narrow audited exception process. Protect builders and publishing roles, retain verification evidence and preserve known-good artifacts. Signing after an uncontrolled rebuild does not restore reproducibility.

e2e: Build from controlled source and dependency inputs using an authorized builder.
Produce the artifact digest, component inventory and provenance linked to that content.
Verify expected signer, builder and source claims before allowing promotion.
Retain the artifact and evidence, then use the inventory to locate affected releases when advisories appear.

tasks.name: Separate three questions
tasks.goal: Avoid substituting one evidence type for another.
steps: Offline, assign component list to SBOM, approved publisher identity to signature verification and build-source relationship to provenance. Explain why none alone proves that the application handles authorization correctly or that its production configuration is secure.

tasks.name: Calculate inventory impact
steps: A fictional SBOM index shows library L in releases A, C and D but not B. From four releases, three require advisory applicability review. Do not claim all three are exploitable; check affected versions, packaging and use separately.

tasks.name: Reject an unrelated signature
tasks.goal: Bind evidence to the right content.
steps: A release expects digest D1 but receives a valid signature for D2. Expected outcome is verification failure for D1. These labels are symbolic, not genuine hashes. Also reject D1 signed only by an identity outside the approved publisher policy.

tasks.name: Design a promotion gate
steps: Specify approved repository, builder identity, immutable digest and required review evidence for a fictional service. Mark missing evidence as blocked or explicitly excepted with owner and expiry, not silently accepted because an SBOM file is attached to the release.

key_terms: SBOM: software bill of materials.
Attestation: statement associated with an artifact.
Provenance: evidence of artifact production.
Verification policy: rules defining acceptable identity and claims.
lesson.safety: Use symbolic artifacts only. Do not generate false attestations, access signing keys or publish signatures for unreviewed releases.
cleanup: Retain the fictional verification policy; no keys, artifacts or attestations were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical release includes an SBOM and a valid signature from an unknown identity. Is that enough to deploy?
interview_points: Verify the exact artifact digest and approved signer.
Inspect expected builder and source provenance.
Treat the SBOM as inventory, not approval.
Apply an explicit gate and documented exception process.

security/sbom-signed-artifacts-provenanc.core: SBOM answers what is included; signatures and provenance provide identity and production evidence under a trust policy. Bind all evidence to the exact digest, protect builders and verify expected claims before promotion.
objectives: Distinguish inventory, signatures and provenance.
Design a digest-bound verification policy.
prerequisites: Understand artifact digests, dependencies and signing identities.

storyboard.title: A valid signature for the wrong artifact cannot authorize release
storyboard.objective: Bind supply-chain evidence to exact content and trusted identity.

scenes.title: Evidence arrives
scenes.caption: The gate checks content and approved identity together.
scenes.narration: The release provides an artifact and associated statements. Verification must bind the expected digest to trusted signer and builder claims.

scenes.title: Digest mismatch
scenes.caption: The signature describes D2, not candidate D1.
scenes.narration: The signature is cryptographically valid but covers different content. Its validity cannot authorize the artifact currently proposed for deployment.

scenes.title: Enforce the actual policy
scenes.caption: Require matching content and authorized production evidence.
scenes.narration: The gate rejects the mismatch and accepts only digest-bound evidence satisfying the approved identity and build-origin policy, or an explicit audited exception.

lesson.title: Network segmentation zero trust and service authorization
lesson.why: A private network limits reachability but does not establish that every reachable caller is trustworthy. An attacker controlling one internal workload can misuse overly broad service permissions unless network boundaries and request authorization work together.
lesson.what: Segmentation restricts communication paths. Zero-trust approaches evaluate identity and context rather than granting implicit trust from location. Service authorization decides which authenticated caller may perform a particular action on a particular resource.

concepts.name: Reachability versus authority
concepts.body: Network rules can prevent one workload from reaching another's port. They cannot generally decide whether an allowed HTTP request may access a specific customer record. Keep transport reachability and application authorization as distinct layers with independently testable policies.

concepts.name: Workload identity
concepts.body: Mutual TLS can authenticate both connection peers using trusted certificates. It protects a transport identity boundary, but the authenticated service still needs action-level permission. Certificate identity mapping and rotation must remain consistent with the service authorization policy.

concepts.name: Default-deny segmentation
concepts.body: Start from required flows and allow only intended peers and protocols within supported policy semantics. Include DNS, telemetry and control-plane dependencies deliberately. A broad allow added to fix one missing dependency can silently restore lateral movement paths that segmentation intended to remove.

concepts.name: Context and review
concepts.body: Authorization may depend on service identity, tenant, operation and resource ownership. Evaluate these attributes on the server, not only in a client interface. Observe denies and policy changes, and review temporary exceptions because topology and legitimate dependency paths evolve.

e2e: The source workload resolves and attempts a connection through allowed network paths.
Peers authenticate through the selected transport and workload identity mechanism.
The destination evaluates the caller's action and resource against application policy.
The service records a useful decision and returns an allowed result or a safe denial.

tasks.name: Build a flow matrix
steps: Offline, allow frontend to API on 443 and API to database on its required port; deny frontend directly to database. Add DNS as an explicit dependency. Explain why the matrix describes reachability but not which records an API caller may read.

tasks.name: Evaluate combined policy
steps: A fictional billing worker has a valid client certificate and network access, but policy permits only invoice.read. It requests invoice.delete. Expected result is denial despite authenticated transport. Both connectivity and authentication can succeed while authorization fails.

tasks.name: Review a temporary exception
steps: A DNS failure is addressed by allowing all egress indefinitely. Reject the broad permanent rule. Identify approved resolver paths and required protocol behavior, then design a scoped exception with owner and expiry while preserving visibility into denied traffic.

tasks.name: Trace compromised internal access
steps: On paper, a compromised reporting service calls a payment API. Require the payment service to check workload identity, permitted operations and tenant scope. Do not perform an attack; describe safe synthetic positive and negative authorization tests.

key_terms: Segmentation: restriction of network communication paths.
mTLS: mutual transport certificate authentication.
Authorization: permission decision for an action and resource.
Lateral movement: access expansion from an initial foothold.
lesson.safety: Use offline policy matrices and fictional identities. Do not probe internal services, issue certificates or change real network policies.
cleanup: Retain the minimal flow matrix and test expectations; no exceptions were installed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical service uses mTLS on a private network but lets every peer perform administrative actions. What control is missing?
interview_points: mTLS authenticates peers but does not grant every action.
Enforce server-side action and resource authorization.
Use least-required network paths as defense in depth.
Review identity mapping, tenant scope and exceptions.

security/network-segmentation-zero-trust.core: Network reachability, transport authentication and application authorization answer different questions. Use required-flow segmentation, verified workload identity and server-side action/resource checks without trusting a caller merely because it is internal.
objectives: Separate reachability, identity and authorization.
Design a least-required service flow matrix.
prerequisites: Understand network filters, certificates and API operations.

storyboard.title: An authenticated peer requests an unauthorized operation
storyboard.objective: Place service authorization after network and identity checks.

scenes.title: Transport succeeds
scenes.caption: The peer identity is valid on an allowed path.
scenes.narration: The worker reaches the service and authenticates through mutual TLS. These checks establish identity and protected connectivity, not unrestricted authority.

scenes.title: Operation exceeds permission
scenes.caption: Read permission does not include delete.
scenes.narration: The worker requests invoice deletion although its policy permits only reading. The service must reject this authenticated but unauthorized operation.

scenes.title: Enforce the resource policy
scenes.caption: Record the denial and retain permitted behavior.
scenes.narration: Server-side authorization denies deletion while allowing legitimate reads, demonstrating why private networking and certificates do not replace action-level checks.

lesson.title: Encryption key management TLS and certificate rotation
lesson.why: Encryption protects data only when key access and identity verification are sound. Rotating a key or certificate without understanding dependent ciphertext and trust paths can create an outage or permanently lose access to retained information.
lesson.what: Encryption uses keys to protect confidentiality and often integrity. Key management governs creation, access, rotation and retirement. TLS certificates support endpoint authentication; their replacement must preserve valid trust and hostname coverage while protecting private keys.

concepts.name: Envelope encryption
concepts.body: A data-encryption key encrypts content, and a key-encryption key protects that data key. This separates bulk data processing from key-management operations. Access to unwrap the data key can expose plaintext, so key-use authorization and audit evidence remain critical.

concepts.name: Rotation versus deletion
concepts.body: Rotating an encryption key does not necessarily rewrite all existing ciphertext. Older key material may be required to decrypt historical data, depending on the service. Disablement or deletion needs an inventory of retained data and recovery implications, not merely a calendar reminder.

concepts.name: TLS certificate lifecycle
concepts.body: Certificates bind identities to public keys through a trusted chain and validity period. Deploy replacements before expiry, verify hostname coverage and ensure clients trust the chain. Reusing a connection can hide a new-handshake failure, so test fresh connections deliberately.

concepts.name: Cryptographic boundaries
concepts.body: Encryption at rest does not stop an authorized application from returning plaintext to the wrong user. TLS protects specific hops, not every internal transfer automatically. Distinguish encryption, integrity, endpoint authentication and authorization when describing what a control actually guarantees.

e2e: Classify protected data and define who may encrypt, decrypt or manage key material.
Encrypt content through the approved envelope or service mechanism and retain key identifiers.
Introduce a replacement key or certificate with documented compatibility and trust checks.
Verify new operations and historical recovery before retiring material that may still be required.

tasks.name: Trace envelope decryption
steps: Draw ciphertext, wrapped data key and key-management service. The application must obtain authorized unwrapping before decrypting data. Explain why possessing encrypted storage files alone differs from having both those files and permission to unwrap their data keys.

tasks.name: Calculate certificate overlap
steps: A fictional certificate expires in 21 days; rollout starts in seven and verification takes two. Remaining margin after verification is 12 days. Test hostname and chain on a fresh connection rather than claiming existing long-lived sessions prove the new certificate works.

tasks.name: Review key retirement
steps: Archive A was encrypted under old key K1 and new writes use K2. Expected conclusion: deleting K1 may make A unreadable unless a supported re-encryption or key-preservation process covers it. The symbolic labels are not actual cryptographic keys.

tasks.name: Separate data access controls
steps: A hypothetical database is encrypted at rest but the API returns another user's records. Identify application authorization as the failed control. Keep encryption enabled while correcting ownership checks; do not suggest changing encryption algorithms to fix the access decision.

key_terms: DEK: key encrypting data content.
KEK: key protecting another key.
Certificate chain: linked trust evidence for an identity.
Rotation: replacement of active cryptographic material.
lesson.safety: Use diagrams and symbolic key names only. Do not generate private keys, access key stores or delete cryptographic material.
cleanup: Retain the retirement checklist; no certificates, keys or encrypted resources were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical team rotates its encryption key and wants to delete the old one immediately. What must be verified first?
interview_points: Inventory historical ciphertext and its key dependencies.
Check the provider's actual rotation and retention behavior.
Verify restoration or supported re-encryption.
Separate rotation from irreversible key deletion.

security/encryption-key-management-tls-a.core: Envelope encryption separates data keys and wrapping keys. Rotation does not imply historical ciphertext no longer needs old material. Verify fresh TLS handshakes, trust chains and hostname coverage; encryption never replaces application authorization.
objectives: Explain envelope-key dependencies.
Plan safe key retirement and certificate overlap.
prerequisites: Understand ciphertext, public/private keys and TLS identity.

storyboard.title: Old ciphertext may still require the old key
storyboard.objective: Explain why key rotation is not immediate safe deletion.

scenes.title: Historical dependency
scenes.caption: The archive's recovery path includes K1.
scenes.narration: The archive was encrypted with material associated with K1, and its current recovery procedure still depends on that key remaining available.

scenes.title: Rotation is mistaken for migration
scenes.caption: New writes using K2 do not necessarily change old ciphertext.
scenes.narration: The team activates K2 and considers deleting K1. That action could strand historical data because rotation alone may not rewrite existing encryption dependencies.

scenes.title: Verify before retirement
scenes.caption: Preserve required material or complete supported migration.
scenes.narration: The owner verifies the service's behavior and tests historical recovery, retaining K1 or completing a supported migration before any irreversible retirement.

lesson.title: Compliance evidence policy enforcement and auditability
lesson.why: A policy document is not evidence that a control operated, and one successful check does not cover every environment forever. Auditability connects requirements to scoped, time-bound records that can be reviewed without exposing unnecessary personal or secret data.
lesson.what: Compliance work maps obligations to controls, owners and evidence. Preventive enforcement blocks disallowed actions, detective controls identify deviations and corrective workflows address them. Technical evidence supports assessment but does not itself issue a legal or independent audit conclusion.

concepts.name: Requirement mapping
concepts.body: Translate broad obligations into concrete control objectives, scope and accountable owners. Different systems may need different implementations. A requirement to restrict access could involve identity review, deployment rules and application authorization rather than a single firewall setting.

concepts.name: Evidence quality
concepts.body: Useful evidence identifies the resource, control version, observation time and outcome. Preserve provenance and access restrictions so records cannot be casually altered. Screenshots without context may omit failures or stale scope and should not be treated as universal proof.

concepts.name: Enforcement stages
concepts.body: Policy can operate before deployment, at admission or after resources exist. Preventive rejection reduces exposure but needs reliable evaluation and an exception path. Detective scans can find legacy drift but do not guarantee that a prohibited action was blocked when it occurred.

concepts.name: Exceptions and retention
concepts.body: Document accepted exceptions with reason, owner, compensating control and expiry. Retain evidence according to applicable obligations and privacy needs, not indefinitely by default. A passing control sample supports only its stated time and population, not every unobserved environment.

e2e: Map a requirement to a measurable control and define its resource scope.
Evaluate or enforce the control using a versioned rule and trusted identity.
Record time, scope, outcome and any approved exception with protected provenance.
Review coverage and expiry, remediate deviations and preserve evidence for the required retention period.

tasks.name: Define a testable control
tasks.goal: Turn policy prose into observable behavior.
steps: For a fictional requirement of reviewed production changes, define evidence as the deployed commit, required approval and matching check result. Do not accept a generic screenshot of a green pipeline that cannot be linked to the actual production revision.

tasks.name: Calculate evidence coverage
steps: A control inventory has 40 in-scope resources, with current evidence for 32. Coverage is 32/40 = 80 percent; eight remain unverified. Do not report compliance as complete merely because every sampled resource passed its check.

tasks.name: Compare preventive and detective controls
steps: A daily scan finds a public resource twelve hours after creation. It provides detective evidence but did not prevent exposure. Add a predeployment or admission rule where appropriate, and retain scanning for existing drift rather than replacing one with an unsupported guarantee.

tasks.name: Review an exception
steps: A fictional exception expired yesterday and lacks a current owner. Mark it for reassessment, not silent renewal. Record the control version, compensating restriction and expiry decision, using resource aliases rather than copying personal information into the evidence record.

key_terms: Control objective: intended protective outcome.
Evidence scope: resources and period covered.
Detective control: mechanism identifying deviations.
Exception: approved bounded departure from policy.
lesson.safety: Use fictional requirements and inventories. Do not access audit archives, export personal data or claim an independent compliance certification.
cleanup: Retain anonymized evidence templates; no production controls, audit records or retention settings were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical dashboard shows every scanned resource passing, but only half the inventory was scanned. What should the report say?
interview_points: State the evaluated population and uncovered resources.
Separate passing results from complete coverage.
Record observation time and control version.
Avoid claiming independent certification from a technical dashboard.

security/compliance-evidence-policy-enfo.core: Map requirements to owned, measurable controls. Evidence needs scope, time, rule version and protected provenance. Distinguish preventive from detective coverage, track exceptions and report unverified resources without overstating compliance.
objectives: Design scoped control evidence.
Calculate coverage and distinguish enforcement timing.
prerequisites: Understand resource inventories, policies and audit records.

storyboard.title: All observed checks pass but the inventory is incomplete
storyboard.objective: Separate control outcomes from evidence coverage.

scenes.title: Scope established
scenes.caption: The requirement covers forty resources.
scenes.narration: The control owner defines the inventory and the rule version, making the population to be evaluated explicit before interpreting results.

scenes.title: Only thirty-two observed
scenes.caption: Passing checks do not cover eight missing resources.
scenes.narration: Every observed resource passes, but evidence exists for only thirty-two. The remaining eight cannot be silently treated as compliant.

scenes.title: Report outcomes and gaps
scenes.caption: State eighty-percent coverage and assign follow-up.
scenes.narration: The report separates passing outcomes from missing evidence, records the observation period and assigns owners to complete the unverified portion.

lesson.title: Kubernetes workload security admission and runtime protection
lesson.why: A safe-looking container image can run with dangerous host access if its pod specification allows it. Kubernetes security must evaluate workload configuration before admission and observe runtime behavior afterward without assuming either layer catches every risk.
lesson.what: Admission controls inspect or modify API requests before persistence. Pod Security Standards describe privilege profiles, while RBAC governs API actions and runtime controls constrain execution. These mechanisms address different boundaries and require compatible workload design.

concepts.name: Admission timing
concepts.body: Admission occurs after authentication and authorization of the API request. Validating controls can reject a disallowed pod specification; mutating controls can set fields. Existing workloads are not automatically repaired merely because a stricter admission policy is later introduced.

concepts.name: Restricted workload settings
concepts.body: Applicable Restricted-profile requirements include nonroot execution, restricted privilege escalation, suitable seccomp and capability limits, with details varying by operating system and policy version. Explicitly configure the intended Linux workload rather than relying on an image username alone to prove its effective identity.

concepts.name: Host and identity boundaries
concepts.body: Host namespaces, privileged execution and sensitive host paths can undermine isolation. Service-account tokens and RBAC determine API authority separately from Linux user identity. Disable unnecessary token mounting and grant only required API actions where the workload needs cluster access.

concepts.name: Runtime and rollout
concepts.body: Runtime monitoring can detect unexpected process, file or network behavior after admission. Detection needs scoped response procedures, not automatic unbounded disruption. Roll out policy in audit or warning modes where supported, review violations and then enforce with controlled exceptions.

e2e: An authenticated caller submits a workload specification through authorized API access.
Admission evaluates the pod against the configured policy version and rejects forbidden settings.
Accepted workloads run under their declared identity and kernel restrictions.
Runtime evidence and periodic inventory reveal behavior or legacy configurations requiring remediation.

tasks.name: Separate three identities
tasks.goal: Avoid equating Linux user with API permission.
steps: Draw the human deploying a pod, the pod's service account and the container's Linux user. Assign API submission authorization, workload API authority and process permissions respectively. Explain why runAsNonRoot does not itself restrict the service account's Kubernetes RBAC grants.

tasks.name: Evaluate a Linux policy checklist
steps: A fictional Linux pod specifies runAsNonRoot true, allowPrivilegeEscalation false and seccomp RuntimeDefault but requests privileged true. Expected decision is reject under a restricted policy; compliant fields do not cancel the explicitly forbidden privilege request. Check the pinned policy version for complete requirements.

tasks.name: Review unnecessary API access
steps: A static web server never calls the Kubernetes API but automatically receives a service-account token. Propose disabling unnecessary token mounting and reviewing its role grants. Do not change a real namespace or assume token removal prevents ordinary application network traffic.

tasks.name: Plan enforcement rollout
tasks.goal: Avoid breaking unknown legacy workloads blindly.
steps: On paper, inventory existing pods, evaluate a pinned policy in audit or warning mode and remediate identified violations before enforcement. Assign exceptions narrowly. Explain why enforcement on new admissions does not automatically rewrite every previously running pod into a compliant form.

key_terms: Admission: API request evaluation before persistence.
RBAC: role-based API authorization.
Seccomp: system-call filtering mechanism.
Pod Security Standards: Kubernetes workload privilege profiles.
lesson.safety: Use offline pod-field reviews only. Do not apply manifests, alter namespace enforcement or attempt container escapes.
cleanup: Retain the synthetic policy checklist; no cluster resources or runtime agents were installed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical pod runs as nonroot but has a powerful service-account token and host mounts. Is it adequately restricted?
interview_points: Separate Linux process identity from API RBAC.
Review host access, privilege escalation, capabilities and seccomp.
Remove unnecessary token access.
Evaluate the complete applicable policy and runtime risk, not one field.

security/kubernetes-workload-security-ad.core: Admission, RBAC and runtime controls protect different boundaries. Evaluate complete versioned Pod Security requirements, host access and service-account authority. Nonroot alone is insufficient, and new enforcement does not automatically repair existing pods.
objectives: Separate admission, workload identity and runtime controls.
Evaluate a restricted workload and staged policy rollout.
prerequisites: Understand pods, service accounts and Linux privileges.

storyboard.title: Nonroot does not cancel a privileged pod request

scenes.title: Authorized API request
scenes.caption: The caller may submit a workload, subject to admission.
scenes.narration: API authorization permits the caller to create pods, but admission still evaluates whether the requested execution configuration satisfies policy.

scenes.title: Conflicting privilege field
scenes.caption: A forbidden field remains forbidden despite other safe settings.
scenes.narration: The pod requests nonroot execution and privileged mode. The safe-looking identity field does not negate the disallowed privileged setting.

scenes.title: Reject and correct the specification
scenes.caption: Review every applicable requirement before resubmission.
scenes.narration: Admission rejects the workload. The author removes unnecessary host privileges and verifies all applicable policy requirements before submitting a corrected specification.

lesson.title: Secure software development and dependency updates
lesson.why: Security work added only at release time discovers expensive design mistakes late. A secure development lifecycle turns threat assumptions, dependency changes and verification into normal engineering work with clear ownership and recoverable releases.
lesson.what: Secure development integrates requirements, design review, implementation checks, dependency management and response readiness. Updates reduce known risk but can introduce incompatibilities, so they need controlled inputs, tests and staged rollout rather than blind automatic acceptance.

concepts.name: Security requirements
concepts.body: Define expected authorization, data handling and failure behavior alongside functional requirements. Use threat models to identify abuse cases early. A requirement such as only owners may read records can become both implementation guidance and a negative test, not merely a final checklist item.

concepts.name: Dependency control
concepts.body: Track direct and transitive dependencies through manifests and lockfiles. Review the actual resolved graph, trusted package sources and lifecycle scripts. Pinning improves reproducibility but freezes vulnerabilities too, so ownership and a regular update process remain necessary.

concepts.name: Review and verification
concepts.body: Review risky changes for data flow, access boundaries and backward compatibility. Combine focused tests, contract checks and relevant security analysis. Generated patches still require inspection; an automated update title does not prove the resolved dependencies or installation behavior are harmless.

concepts.name: Release and response
concepts.body: Promote identified artifacts through staged rollout with health and error signals, retaining a compatible rollback or forward-repair path. Record accepted risks and response contacts. A vulnerability disclosure needs triage and remediation communication rather than silently deleting evidence of the affected release.

e2e: Translate security requirements and abuse cases into design and acceptance tests.
Review dependency changes and resolved inputs before building an identified artifact.
Run the relevant functional, compatibility and security checks with truthful evidence.
Release gradually, monitor intended signals and respond to new findings through an owned update process.

tasks.name: Write a negative requirement
steps: For a fictional notes API, specify that user A cannot read user B's note even when its identifier is known. Pair a denied cross-user test with an allowed own-note test, both using synthetic fixtures rather than real accounts.

tasks.name: Calculate update scope
steps: A proposed update changes one direct library and four transitive packages. Expected review scope is five changed components, not one. Compare the lockfile diff and relevant advisories, and identify any new installation scripts or package sources before approval.

tasks.name: Choose targeted verification
tasks.goal: Test compatibility at the affected boundary.
steps: A fictional HTTP-client update changes timeout exceptions. Add unit coverage for exception handling and an isolated integration test for timeout behavior. Do not claim the update safe solely because the package manager resolved dependencies successfully or an unrelated test passed.

tasks.name: Plan staged release recovery
steps: Release the hypothetical update to a small isolated stage, observe timeout errors and latency, and retain the known compatible artifact. If data migrations are involved, document forward repair or compatibility before assuming that deploying the old binary reverses every effect.

key_terms: SDLC: software development lifecycle.
Lockfile: recorded dependency resolution.
Transitive dependency: dependency required indirectly.
Acceptance criterion: observable condition defining intended behavior.
lesson.safety: Use paper changes and synthetic tests. Do not install unreviewed packages, execute dependency scripts or update production applications.
cleanup: Retain the fictional update checklist and pending evidence fields; no dependencies or deployments were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical automated dependency update changes one manifest line and is marked low risk. What else should be reviewed?
interview_points: Inspect the resolved transitive graph and lockfile.
Check package sources, lifecycle behavior and advisories.
Test affected API and error-handling contracts.
Use identified artifacts and staged rollout with a credible recovery path.

security/secure-software-development-and.core: Build security requirements into design and tests. Dependency pinning supports reproducibility but needs owned updates. Review the resolved graph, verify affected contracts and stage identified artifacts with monitored recovery rather than trusting automation labels.
objectives: Translate abuse cases into acceptance tests.
Review direct and transitive dependency update risk.
prerequisites: Understand dependency manifests, tests and releases.

storyboard.title: One manifest change updates several transitive components
storyboard.objective: Trace dependency review through the resolved graph.

scenes.title: Small visible edit
scenes.caption: The manifest changes one direct library version.
scenes.narration: An automated update proposes a small manifest edit, but the actual build inputs depend on the full resolved dependency graph.

scenes.title: Hidden scope expands
scenes.caption: Four transitive packages change too.
scenes.narration: The lockfile reveals additional components and possible lifecycle changes. Reviewing only the one-line manifest would miss most changed inputs.

scenes.title: Review and verify the actual inputs
scenes.caption: Test affected behavior before a staged release.
scenes.narration: The team reviews all changed components, checks affected contracts and promotes an identified artifact through a monitored stage with explicit recovery planning.
